objectives: Decode short controlled sentences containing taught CVC patterns.
Answer literal comprehension questions using sentence evidence.
Identify who, what and sequence information in controlled text.
concepts: Text evidence comes directly from the words read.
Rereading supports accuracy, phrasing and fluency.

definitions.definition: Words in a sentence that directly support an answer.
Understanding and responding to what has been read.
Reading accurately, smoothly and with appropriate phrasing.

workedExamples: Read “Wag can tag.” Ask what Wag can do; the answer is tag.
Read “The web is wet.” Identify the subject and its description.
Reread “Wig is big.” to make the sentence smooth and accurate.
commonMistakes: Answering from memory instead of the sentence.

basic: Read short w-CVC sentences and identify explicit details.
conceptual: Match questions to evidence in a sentence.
application: Answer who/what questions from controlled text.
higherOrderThinking: Explain why rereading helps confirm meaning.
mixedReview: Mix decoding, sentence comprehension and word-family review.

quickRevision: read → check words → find evidence → answer → reread
mistakeBasedRevision: If an answer is unsupported, reread the sentence and locate the exact words that support it.
weakTopicRevision: Practise the question type—who, what or sequence—that causes difficulty.

outcomes: Learner decodes controlled w-CVC sentences accurately.
Learner answers literal comprehension questions using text evidence.
Learner rereads controlled sentences with improved fluency.

questions.question: Read: “Wag can tag.” What can Wag do?
Read: “Wig is big.” Which word describes Wig?
Read: “Win can sit.” Who can sit?
Read: “The web is wet.” What is wet?
Which sentence tells what the web is like?
What should you do to find an answer in a controlled sentence?
Read: “Wag can tag. Wag can sit.” What can Wag do?
Read: “The web is wet.” Which word comes first?
Read: “Wig is big.” What is the rime in wig?
Read: “Win can sit.” Which word names the person or character?
A learner says “Wag can wet” instead of “Wag can tag.” What should they do?
options: look at the final sounds and reread
